title: N-Repeated Element in Size 2N Array
spaceBreakdown:
- no containers or arrays allocated
- no recursion
- not counted: input vector, returned int
approach: The repeated element appears n times among 2n positions, while n other distinct values appear once each. By the pigeonhole principle, two copies of the repeated value must sit within distance 2 of each other (for n≥3; n=2 is handled by the fallback). Scan left to right, comparing each element to the one and two positions before it; the first match is the answer. If no match is found, the only close pair was at indices 0 and 1, so return nums[0].
hints: With n copies of one value placed among 2n slots and only n distinct other values available to separate them, how far apart can two consecutive copies of the repeated value be?
Compare each element to the previous one and the one before that; the first equal pair is the answer. In [5,1,5,2,5,3,5,4], index 2 (value 5) equals index 0 (value 5), so return 5.

**Distance-2 only pair** - two copies of the repeated value are separated by exactly one other element.
`Input: nums = [3,1,3,2]` → `Expected: 3`
⚠️ Bug: comparing only nums[i] to nums[i-1] (adjacent only) and returning -1 on no match → returns -1 instead of 3.

**Repeated pair at start** - the only close pair is at indices 0 and 1.
`Input: nums = [3,3,1,2]` → `Expected: 3`
⚠️ Bug: returning nums.back() as the fallback when no match is found → returns 2 instead of 3.

**Match at last index** - the equal pair is found at the final comparison.
`Input: nums = [1,2,3,3]` → `Expected: 3`
⚠️ Bug: loop condition `i < n - 1` (off-by-one) → never checks i=3, returns fallback nums[0]=1 instead of 3.

**Gap of 3 with n=2** - the minimum n allows the two copies to be three apart.
`Input: nums = [3,1,2,3]` → `Expected: 3`
⚠️ Bug: assuming a distance-≤2 pair always exists and returning -1 on no match → returns -1 instead of 3.

followUps.q: The array arrives as a stream too large to store. How do you find the repeated element?
followUps.a: Keep only the last three elements in a sliding window. Compare each incoming element to the previous two; the first match is the answer. This uses O(1) space and one pass, same as the in-memory version.

followUps.q: Instead of one element repeated n times, suppose k distinct elements are each repeated and you must return all of them. How does the approach change?
followUps.a: The pigeonhole guarantee no longer holds, so switch to a frequency hash map and return every element with count greater than one. This costs O(n) time and O(n) space.

followUps.q: What if nums[i] ranges over the full 32-bit signed integers, including negatives?
followUps.a: The distance-2 comparison never depends on the value range, so the same code works unchanged with O(n) time and O(1) space.
